name: Our contribution: connect the cellular mechanisms to the par

text:
SPEAKER SCRIPT

We want to understand how short electric pulses change EV release, and how a model can help us plan the next experiment. A particle count on its own can have several explanations. Cells may release more vesicles, repair their membranes, or shed particles as they become injured. Some particles may also disappear before we collect the sample. We built a model that brings these processes together and compares their combined effect with laboratory measurements. The goal is to explore possible explanations for the response and identify which additional measurements would be most useful. I will show the biology we included, how the model compares with our current data, and how it can guide the next study.

PRESENTER CUE
Introduce extracellular vesicles as EVs. Emphasize what the model can provide to an experimental study.

title: The biological steps included in the model

name: The framework we developed
text: The biological steps included in the model

SPEAKER SCRIPT

This overview shows the biology we brought into the model. The electric pulse affects the cell membrane and internal compartments. That can change calcium signals, cell stress and repair. Those changes can then affect how vesicles form and leave the cell, as well as how much unwanted material accompanies them. Cell type and cell condition can influence the whole response. Bringing these steps together lets us ask how a change in one part could affect what we eventually collect. The diagram also includes possible changes in vesicle contents and activity. Those parts remain early estimates rather than experimentally confirmed outcomes in this study.

name: Python simulator, reproducible parameter snapshots, calibrat
text: The model explores how release, particle loss and measurement shape the final count.

SPEAKER SCRIPT

We organize the model around the same questions an experimentalist would ask. What pulse did the cells receive? How did the cells respond? What did they release? What reached the final sample? The distinction on the right is especially useful. Particles can leave a cell and then disappear from the medium before collection. Collection and measurement can change the count again. That means a change in the assay result does not automatically tell us how secretion changed. The model gives us a way to explore these steps separately, compare their combined effect with the data, and decide which part needs a direct measurement.

PRESENTER CUE
Emphasize the difference between what cells release and what reaches the assay.

Here, blue shows the measured size profiles and pink shows the model after we adjusted it using the available data. The example follows the three-pulse condition at thirty minutes, one hour and three hours. The model reproduces the main group of particles around one hundred to one hundred sixty nanometers. It also leaves a clear gap at the one-hour peak. That gap is useful because it shows where our current explanation is incomplete and where extra measurements could help. preview: What the model helps us ask | How this helps an experiment

text:
SPEAKER SCRIPT

For an experimentalist, the useful outcome is help choosing the next measurement. We vary the model inputs to see which changes could alter the particle count, then ask whether the available data can tell those explanations apart. In this dataset, release, disappearance from the medium, and particle recovery all need attention. The size measurements also cannot reliably tell us how much of the signal comes from dying cells. That gives us a reason to collect cell-injury measurements alongside particle counts. More generally, this approach helps focus experiments on processes that may change the time course and on gaps that make the results difficult to interpret. These are early priorities to test. Their order depends on the model assumptions and does not yet establish which biological process is truly most important.

PRESENTER CUE
Lead with the experimental benefit. Particle recovery was provisionally fixed at one in fitting, with uncertainty absorbed into source scales. Recovery itself was not independently estimated. The original Gii diagnostic is intentionally replaced by its experimental implications.

SPEAKER SCRIPT

The next study can make the model much more useful by adding measurements that separate the possible explanations. First, measure how collection and processing affect particle recovery, and confirm the pulse settings and culture volume. Second, add matched controls and more collection times between one and three hours. That will help us examine whether cells keep releasing particles or whether particles disappear from the medium. Third, pair size profiles with EV markers, calcium responses and cell-injury measurements, so the particle signal has a clearer biological meaning. Finally, use additional pulse conditions to test predictions on new data. The value of the model is that it gives us a structured way to compare explanations and choose the next measurements.

PRESENTER CUE
Connect each measurement with the explanation it would help test. This is an early measurement plan, not a statistically powered study design.

title: What changes when we add more pulses?

text: What changes when we add more pulses?
A larger pulse train can prolong calcium signaling and increase injury.
Illustrative simulations. Cargo, viability and recovered output are model scores.

SPEAKER SCRIPT

Here we change only the number of pulses. Each pulse has the same field, width and spacing. Deposited energy rises, while the voltage reached during one pulse stays the same. The model then shows a larger and longer calcium response as the train gets larger. That does not translate into a simple increase in small-vesicle release: the viability score also falls. For an experiment, this comparison suggests measuring early calcium recovery and cell injury alongside vesicle output when choosing pulse number. Heating is shown only indirectly through the energy descriptor; the current equations do not establish that heating caused the injury. These patterns are hypotheses to test, not a calibrated dose recommendation.

title: Calcium clearance changes the cell response

text: Calcium clearance changes the cell response
A prolonged calcium response can increase injury even with the same pulses.
Illustrative simulations. Cargo, viability and recovered output are model scores.

SPEAKER SCRIPT

The first two columns are identical because the exposure is identical. This time we change only the capacities of three calcium-removal pathways. With lower clearance capacity, calcium remains elevated longer and the model assigns more injury. The repair activity also lasts longer, which should be read as a sustained demand for repair rather than evidence that the cell is healthier. A larger release signal can therefore accompany a less favorable cell state. This is useful for planning experiments: the decay of the calcium response may tell us more than its peak alone. The protein cargo score changes very little here because it uses the terminal cell state. The model has not identified these rows with actual cell types.

title: Vesicle machinery can change release and cargo

text: Vesicle machinery can change release and cargo
Vesicle pathway settings change small-EV release and modeled protein cargo.
Illustrative simulations. Cargo, viability and recovered output are model scores.

SPEAKER SCRIPT

In this comparison, exposure, calcium clearance and repair settings all stay the same. We change three parts of the vesicle machinery together: maturation, vesicle formation and docking. The calcium and repair traces therefore overlap. Farther to the right, the small-vesicle output and protein cargo score rise, while the viability score is almost unchanged. The point is that increasing electrical exposure is not the only possible way to alter output. The model can help formulate pathway experiments that ask whether vesicle production can be adjusted separately from cell stress. The cargo column is a simple model score; it does not establish a measured protein change or a functional benefit.

The same biological release can give different recovered yields.
Illustrative simulations. Cargo, viability and recovered output are model scores.

SPEAKER SCRIPT

Every biological setting is identical in these three rows. The only change is the fraction assumed to be recovered during isolation. The first seven columns should therefore be identical, and they are. Only the final yield changes: a process that recovers sixty percent gives six times the small-vesicle yield of one that recovers ten percent. For an experimentalist, this is a reminder to measure process recovery before assigning an output difference to the cell. It also shows how the framework separates a biological hypothesis from a process assumption. These efficiencies are examples, not claims about particular isolation methods. This final column uses cumulative release rather than the separate medium-stock and sampling model.

WHAT CHANGES
10% recovery: Only isolation_efficiency changes to 0.1; every biological setting and the isolation method factor of 1 are unchanged. The modeled harvest horizon is 0.5 h.
30% recovery: Only isolation_efficiency changes to 0.3; every biological setting and the isolation method factor of 1 are unchanged. The modeled harvest horizon is 0.5 h.

FIGURE CAPTION
Isolation-only negative control. Assumed isolation efficiency is 10%, 30% or 60%, with all upstream inputs unchanged. Modules 1–7 therefore remain identical. The final column applies that efficiency to cumulative small-EV release; it is not extracellular medium stock, assay concentration or a comparison of named isolation methods. The eight columns show, respectively: deposited energy (J/mL); single-pulse plasma-membrane voltage (V); cytosolic calcium (µM, 0–60 s); repair activity (0–1 score, 0–60 s); cumulative small-EV release (relative model units, 0–30 min); protein cargo enrichment (terminal model score at 30 min); viability score (%, derived from peak modeled damage); and recovered small-EV yield (relative model units at 30 min). Energy, voltage, cargo, viability and recovery are scalar bars; calcium, repair and release are time courses. Axes match across all five figures. Input labels identify dependencies of the selected plotted readout, rather than every output of the module. The displayed recovered small-EV yield depends on cumulative release and assumed recovery; other process objectives also use cargo and quality. All runs use a 30-min horizon and 0.25-s output interval. Module titles: 1. Pulse delivery, exposure geometry and dosimetry; 2. Plasma membrane and organelle electrodynamics; 3. Ion transport, Ca²⁺ mobilization, ROS and bioenergetics; 4. Ca²⁺-dependent remodeling and repair; 5. EV biogenesis and subtype release; 6. Cargo sorting, EV composition and potency; 7. Injury, debris and quality gate; 8. Manufacturing, isolation and QC interface. These are illustrative simulations with provisional, uncalibrated parameters, not validated treatment recommendations or predictions for a named cell type. Deposited energy is an exposure descriptor. Heating is not coupled back into the injury equations, so the model cannot establish heat-caused injury. The reduced model uses a single-pulse charging descriptor and an effective perturbation duration; it does not resolve every nanosecond pulse or bipolar cancellation. The remodeling/repair score is algebraic and does not feed back to close pores or repair the damage state in this implementation. Release and recovered yield are relative model units, not calibrated particle counts. The protein cargo score is a terminal enrichment proxy, not measured cargo or function. The viability score is derived from peak modeled damage over the simulation; it is not a measured survival percentage or the recovered end-state. Recovered small-EV yield is the Layer 8 transform of cumulative release and assumed isolation efficiency. It is not extracellular medium stock or a sampling model.

INTERPRETATION
Bars in modules 1 and 2 summarize exposure and charging. Modules 3 and 4 show the first 60 s. Module 5 shows cumulative small-EV release over 30 min in relative pathway units. Cargo is an exploratory endpoint score, viability uses peak simulated damage, and manufacturing applies a recovery multiplier to cumulative release rather than harvesting the extracellular stock. Couplings branch: column order is not a strictly serial pathway. Heating is diagnostic and does not drive cellular injury in this implementation. Repair activation does not dynamically reseal pores or change the damage-repair coefficient.
